subject: Retention examples: what persists vs auto-purge (follow-up)
messages:

Subject: Quick Q on what Redwood keeps by default (examples)

Hi Tessa,

Thanks for the demo last week — Everclear is close to making a procurement decision, and our security team has a couple of follow-up questions that need concrete examples for the contract. We want short example scenarios showing what Redwood retains by default vs what gets auto-purged immediately or on customer request. Specifically:

- For hosted API: do you keep full request and response bodies by default? If so, for how long?
- Differentiation between prompt (original user text) and generated output — are both treated the same?
- Streaming/chunked responses: are intermediate chunks persisted?
- KV/LLM cache or session state: transient or stored?
- Attachments uploaded via the API: do you keep file contents or just references/metadata?

A short, example-driven reply would be ideal (e.g., two-three bullet scenarios). Also attaching the security questionnaire we circulated — the highlighted sections on retention are what our procurement team will push on.

Appended: [Attachment: Everclear_Security_Questionnaire_v2.pdf (pdf, 340KB)]

Thanks,
Elena

Hi Elena — thanks for the clear asks and for sending the questionnaire. Below are concrete examples and the short answers up front; I’m looping in Karthik (privacy) and Marissa (product) for technical detail and a one-page summary we can attach.

Short answers (hosted API):
- Default: full request + generated response bodies are captured for short-term operational troubleshooting.
- Default retention window (hosted): 60 days for request/response artifacts; prompt/inputs and generated outputs are categorized but both live within that window unless customer opts out.
- Streaming fragments and ephemeral KV cache are transient and not persisted as separate long-lived artifacts by default.
- Attachments: we store file metadata and a customer-flagged copy only when needed for features (search, retrieval); otherwise references/metadata are retained.

Examples:
1) Production debug: Customer calls /v1/generate with user prompt and model output. We retain the request and response payloads for 60 days to investigate anomalies. After 60 days the artifacts are scheduled for deletion (subject to legal hold exceptions).

2) Short session KV: A chat session uses KV cache for latency; cache is in-memory on the serving pod and not written to blob storage unless the customer configures session persistence.

3) Streaming case: A long-running stream returns partial tokens. We assemble the final output for storage (if retention enabled); individual token-chunk intermediates are not persisted by default.

Next steps: Marissa will attach a one-page summary you can hand to procurement and Karthik will add the deletion ticket path (API + support workflow). I attached a draft summary to this thread.

Attachment: [redwood-retention-summary-draft.md (text, 6KB)]

—Tessa
Tessa Morgan
Solutions Director, Redwood Inference

Hi Elena — adding the retention/delete runbook details and a few technical clarifications. I’ll keep this high-level so it’s procurement-friendly but actionable.

Retention categories (hosted API defaults):
- Request metadata (headers, timestamps, routing): retained 90 days for operational tracing. Examples: request id, client IP (anonymized where applicable), timestamp.
- Request/response bodies (prompts and generated outputs): retained 60 days by default for hosted customers to allow debugging and quality evaluations. Both inputs and outputs are treated as "stored artifacts" but we tag each artifact ("input" vs "output") to support filtering and purge.
- Model derivatives / telemetry (aggregate metrics, token counts): persisted longer for platform health (default 365 days) and stored as aggregated/anonymous metrics — not tied to raw prompt text.
- Streaming intermediates & KV caches: ephemeral — in-memory on serving nodes and not written to durable blob storage unless the customer enables session persistence or explicit artifact saving.
- Attachments uploaded via the API: by default we keep file metadata (filename, size, MIME) and a content hash. The file content itself is retained only if the customer enables retrieval/search features; otherwise we keep only the metadata for 60 days.

Deletion pathways:
- Self-serve: Customers can use the Admin Console to purge artifacts by time range or artifact type (input/output/attachments). Purge requests start synchronous removal from indexes and async deletion from durable stores; typical completion time: 24–72 hours depending on dataset size.
- API: We provide a /v1/data/delete endpoint (token-auth) that accepts filters (date range, artifact-type). Successful requests return a purge ticket id.
- Manual/legal: For items impacted by legal hold or audit, we coordinate with the customer and the Redwood Compliance team; this can extend the timeline.

Example scenarios (quick):
A) Customer requests deletion of a single conversation created last month — they call /v1/data/delete for that conversation id. We mark the artifact for immediate de-indexing and complete background blob deletion within 48 hours.
B) Customer requests org-wide purge for the last year — this begins a multi-step runbook: index sweep, queued blob deletes, and a confirmation report when done (SLA varies by size; typical mid-size org completes within 5–7 days).

Dedicated & Private (VPC/on-prem): Customers control retention via their deployment configuration and can set retention to 0 days (no stored artifacts) or mirror hosted defaults; Redwood’s private control plane can also be configured to enforce retention policies if asked.

Audit evidence & procurement asks:
- We can provide an attestation letter describing hosted default retention windows (+ exceptions) and a runbook excerpt on purge timelines.
- SOC 2 artifacts and our deletion playbook are available under an NDA / standard procurement channel.

If you’d like, I can convert the above into a short table for your procurement packet.

—Karthik
Karthik Iyer
Privacy & Compliance Lead, Redwood Inference
